query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the degree of short‐range order (SRO) in equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi and selected quaternary subsets via tailored thermomechanical treatments elevates local stacking fault energy variations, which in turn modify dislocation mobility and the relative activation of twinning versus full dislocation slip. This microstructural tuning is hypothesized to govern the observed differences in yield strength, strain-hardening behavior, and ductility relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy processed to achieve a stable single-phase FCC structure, along with selected quaternary subsets derived by omitting one element.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled annealing (at 500–700 °C for varied durations) followed by rapid quenching to selectively tune the degree of SRO without altering the overall FCC phase, combined with in situ TEM tensile testing to capture real-time dislocation mechanisms.
generation.conditions: Thermomechanical processing that ensures retention of the single-phase FCC structure; mechanical testing performed under strain-controlled uniaxial tension at room temperature (and, if needed, at moderate elevated temperatures, e.g. up to 300 °C) with identical strain rates across samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of short‐range chemical order (SRO) at the atomic scale, as quantified by diffuse scattering or related diffraction methods.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced SRO changes the local chemical environment, which modulates the stacking fault energies in different regions of the alloy. These variations alter the energetic barriers for dislocation nucleation, glide, and twinning, thereby shifting the balance between strength (via increased yield stress and work-hardening) and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, alloys processed to increase SRO will exhibit a higher yield strength, altered strain-hardening behavior (potentially with increased twin density or modified dislocation arrangements), and changes in ductility. These differences will be corroborated by diffraction measurements (indicating higher levels of SRO) and by in situ TEM imaging that reveals modified dislocation slip patterns and twin formation.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy prepared under standard thermomechanical conditions exhibiting established single-phase FCC structure and typical dislocation/twinning behavior.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to apply to FCC single-phase high-entropy and medium-entropy alloys processed such that phase separation and precipitate formation are suppressed; its validity may be limited under extreme deformation rates, very high temperatures, or in systems where secondary phases emerge.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence suggests that SRO can modestly increase yield strength, the quantitative relationship between the degree of SRO, local stacking fault energy variations, and dislocation/twinning activity remains uncertain. Additionally, sensitivity to precise processing parameters and compositional fluctuations introduces uncertainty in the magnitude of the effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi and selected quaternary alloys subjected to a range of controlled annealing/quenching cycles to achieve different degrees of SRO. Characterize the SRO quantitatively using X-ray or neutron diffuse scattering. Conduct in situ TEM tensile tests on these samples under identical strain rate and temperature conditions to monitor dislocation mobility, stacking fault formation, and twinning behavior.
measurements: Quantitative measurement of SRO via diffuse scattering intensity and pair correlation functions.
Yield strength and strain-hardening rate from mechanical testing.
Direct imaging of dislocation slip, partial dislocation separation, and twin density via in situ TEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic variations in the degree of SRO (as confirmed by diffraction techniques) do not correlate with changes in dislocation behavior (e.g., stacking fault width, twin activation) and do not produce the predicted modifications in yield strength and strain-hardening behavior relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, then the proposed mechanistic link between SRO and mechanical-property differences would be falsified.

In addition to twinning activities and GPFE curves, we further investigated the dislocation morphology and mobility at a constant strain rate or shear stress, with results indicating that there was a higher barrier for achieving equivalent dislocation velocity in HEAs than in Ni (Supplementary Fig. 9). The extended dislocation in HEA exhibited rugged dislocation lines and a significantly varied dissociation width, which differed markedly from that in Ni with smooth straight dislocation lines and a uniform SF width. Dislocation glide in the HEA was enabled via a series of forward slips by local segments after depinning from local heterogeneities,, and this resulted in nontrivial fluctuations in shear stress under a constant strain rate or in dislocation velocity under constant shear stress. The distinct dislocation behavior of the HEA is essentially pertinent to the severe lattice distortion due to the different atomic sizes and intrinsic properties of individual constituent elements,. We chose the FCC MEA NiCoCr as a model because it is a representative of multi-principal element systems and its mechanical properties are typical of (and often better than) other quaternary and quinary HEAs,. To enable insightful large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, which are sorely needed to provide atomistic insight about dislocation behavior and adequate statistics, but have thus far been lacking in the HEA field, we developed an empirical interatomic potential for NiCoCr alloys without consideration of spin polarization (Methods). proposals.material_system: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi baseline and selected quaternary subsets
proposals.intervention: Tailored thermomechanical treatments (controlled annealing/quenching cycles) aimed at systematically tuning short‐range chemical order (SRO) without changing the overall phase
proposals.conditions: Annealing at intermediate temperatures (500–700 °C) for varied times followed by rapid quenching, ensuring single-phase FCC retention
proposals.structural_mediator: Degree of short‐range ordering/clustering at the atomic scale
proposals.mechanism: Variations in SRO modify local stacking fault energies and influence dislocation mobility/twinning, thus altering the balance between yield strength and ductility
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic quinary baseline, alloys exhibiting higher SRO should show an increase in yield strength and possible changes in strain-hardening behavior, while those with reduced SRO should display more uniform deformation; these differences will be quantifiable via diffraction (e.g., diffuse scattering) and mechanical testing
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It tests whether local chemical order, modulated by processing, governs the complex interplay of strength and failure behavior, thereby resolving part of the unresolved differences among the candidate alloys and informing cost-performance trade-offs by linking processing parameters to microstructural evolution

proposals.material_system: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi baseline versus selected ternary subsets
proposals.intervention: Grain-boundary engineering through controlled sub-solvus annealing to promote or suppress segregation at grain boundaries
proposals.conditions: Heat treatments at temperatures just below the solidus (e.g., 600–750 °C) for defined durations followed by controlled cooling, ensuring minimal phase transformation
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain boundary chemistry and local compositional inhomogeneity
proposals.mechanism: Subtle segregation of specific elements at grain boundaries influences dislocation emission and crack initiation; altered boundary chemistries can either impede or facilitate dislocation sliding, affecting the overall ductility and fracture toughness
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic baseline, ternary alloys engineered to minimize deleterious segregation should display enhanced ductility and delayed crack initiation, observable via atom probe tomography and in situ mechanical testing
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By isolating the role of grain-boundary segregation, this investigation pinpoints a microstructural feature that may govern the mechanical-property differences and ties in constituent cost (as cheaper elements might segregate differently) with performance

proposals.material_system: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi baseline and strategically designed subsets with modified atomic size distributions (e.g., removing one element to create a ternary or quaternary alloy with reduced misfit)
proposals.intervention: Compositional modification to vary the atomic size misfit parameter and lattice distortion, complemented with identical thermomechanical processing
proposals.conditions: Processing under identical rolling and annealing schedules (e.g., hot rolling followed by annealing at ~800 °C) to achieve fully recrystallized single-phase FCC structures
proposals.structural_mediator: Local lattice strain fields associated with atomic size misfit
proposals.mechanism: Variations in lattice distortion change the local stress fields and thereby influence dislocation nucleation and mobility; increased distortion is expected to hinder dislocation glide and elevate strength but may reduce ductility
proposals.predicted_outcome: Alloys with reduced lattice distortion (lower misfit) will likely exhibit lower yield strength and increased ductility compared to the equiatomic baseline, measurable via X-ray diffraction peak broadening and mechanical tests such as nanoindentation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It provides a mechanistic path linking atomic-level misfit to macroscopic deformation behavior, offering a quantifiable parameter (misfit strain) that can balance performance versus cost by adjusting constituent selection

proposals.material_system: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi baseline and targeted subsets (e.g., quaternary systems omitting Mn or Fe)
proposals.intervention: In situ deformation studies using TEM on samples prepared under identical thermomechanical histories to characterize active dislocation slip systems and stacking fault energies
proposals.conditions: Strain-controlled uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (e.g., 25–300 °C) under controlled strain rates, with simultaneous in situ TEM imaging
proposals.structural_mediator: Spatial distribution of stacking faults, twin boundaries, and partial dislocation activity
proposals.mechanism: Subtle compositional changes alter the stacking fault energy, modulating the relative activation of full dislocation glide versus partial slip/twinning; this shift in deformation mechanism is proposed to be a critical factor in the observed differences in strength and failure behavior
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, subsets with modified stacking fault energies will exhibit distinct dislocation structures (e.g., lower twin density or differing partial dislocation separations), which correlate with variations in strain hardening and ductility
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By directly linking compositional adjustments to changes in dislocation behavior and slip system activation, this study tests a mechanistic hypothesis that can account for diverse mechanical responses while informing cost-performance optimization strategies

decision.rationale: Both candidate directions A and B address the unresolved mechanical-property differences by proposing a link between atomic-scale chemical order and dislocation-mediated plasticity, but from complementary perspectives. Direction A posits that shifting the short‐range order (SRO) via controlled thermomechanical treatments modifies local stacking fault energies and thereby alters slip and twinning behavior. Direction B independently proposes using in situ TEM to directly observe how slight compositional modifications alter dislocation mechanisms and stacking fault distributions. Merging these approaches allows the investigation to (1) systematically tune SRO via tailored annealing/quenching processes while (2) directly correlating the induced atomic-scale ordering with changes in dislocation activity as imaged in situ. This joint strategy directly tests whether processing-controlled SRO is the structural mediator that modulates the deformation mechanisms governing strength and ductility differences, and relates these effects back to cost-performance considerations through processing and constituent selection. Although prior evidence indicates that SRO may only subtly modify yield strength (e.g., PMC10656519), combining it with direct observation of dislocation behavior (as in PMC4682111 and others) offers a robust, multi-scale test of the mechanistic hypothesis.
